rich_summary: After hearing the legend of the cosmic fish, Yudhishthira asks the immortal sage Markandeya to explain the deeper causes of creation and destruction, since the sage has witnessed many cosmic cycles. Markandeya begins by praising the supreme being—Janardana (Vishnu)—the eternal source who creates and withdraws the universe. He explains the vast cycles of time: the four Yugas and the immense “day of Brahma.” As the Kali Yuga declines, social order collapses—truth fades, castes abandon their duties, rulers become corrupt, famine spreads, and morality decays. Eventually cosmic destruction arrives: multiple suns dry the earth, a universal fire consumes creation, and immense clouds flood the world for years. Markandeya recounts wandering alone across the cosmic ocean until he sees a mysterious divine child on a banyan tree. Entering the child’s body, he beholds the entire universe within, revealing Vishnu’s infinite cosmic nature and the illusion (maya) of creation.

highlight_spans.why: Closing lines of the Fish legend emphasize purification through hearing sacred cosmic history.
Explanation of the Yuga system and cosmic time cycles that structure Hindu cosmology.
Description of moral and social collapse during the end of Kali Yuga, a vivid prophecy of degeneration.
The striking vision of the divine child on the banyan tree after the universal flood—one of the most famous theophanies in the epic.

top_scenes.scene_text: Markandeya wandering alone over an endless cosmic ocean after the destruction of the universe until he sees a vast banyan tree with a radiant divine child resting upon it.
The apocalypse of the world: seven blazing suns drying the earth while the fire of Samvartaka consumes forests and mountains beneath storm-filled skies.
Inside the divine child’s body, Markandeya beholds the entire universe—rivers, mountains, cities, gods, and creatures—contained within the cosmic being.
